How Can Marketing Ship to Production?

AppOS architecture, learning from your phone

Stephan Schmidt · Amazing CTO

How can marketing ship to production?

  • Many orgs face the reality of everyone vibe coding
  • Engineering is the new bottleneck for reviews
    • Agents write more code than senior engineers can review
  • Saying no doesn't work, people deploy to Vercel on their own
  • How can engineering feel safe and trust the code?
  • Everyone coding is the biggest lever for productivity and time to market

Your iPhone has solved this

  • You trust code from unknown developers with your bank account
  • iOS and Android have app permissions
    • apps only do what they are allowed to do
  • App Store review checks apps for bad or malicious behavior

AppOS Principles

  • Adapt that model to applications: apps written by marketing, a shell/kernel owned by engineering
  • Possible architectures
    • WASM gives the strongest isolation inside one process
    • Plugins and modules are easier, but the language has to hold the boundary
    • Services put a network between app and shell, a gateway checks permissions

From marketing code to production

AppOS architecture

AI code needs to pass more authorizations

Permissions

  • Every app declares capabilities like pods-read or bookings-write in its manifest
  • The manifest is negotiated: nobody approves permissions one by one
  • A deploy that uses an API not in the manifest is refused
  • Roles still apply: an app with pods-write doesn't let Alice write if she is not allowed to
  • Business rules stay in the platform, like one booking per pod and hour
  • People only review the permissions

Automatic App Review ("Hardening")1

  • Every app is checked before it runs
    • manifest, host function catalog and the code
  • Quality before malice:
    • Apple rejected 1.93M of 7.77M apps in 2024, 1.24M for crashes and bugs, ~43k for hidden features
  • Fuzzing with fake host functions (planned)
    • Finds crashes, n+1 queries, corrupted data, security holes and "DDoS"
  • Pass or fail, no human bottleneck
  • It catches mistakes early, the sandbox still enforces every rule
  1. Apple, App Store Transparency Report 2024

Runtime Sandbox ("Harness")

  • Each request runs in a fresh sandbox without files, network or a database of its own
  • The app reaches the world only through the host functions its manifest grants
  • Every call checks the app's grant and the user's role
  • Every request has a budget for I/O, time, CPU and memory
    • Over budget, the app's slot shows unavailable and the page still renders
    • Five failures in a minute roll the app back automatically
  • App HTML can't run scripts, the shell sets a strict CSP
  • A broken app can't take down the shell or other apps

Gardening

  • Everyone deploys: the CEO to Vercel, a marketer to Fly.io
    • then the marketer leaves
  • Shadow apps keep running and hold data, but nobody knows about them or patches them
  • With AppOS we know what runs, who owns it and what it may do
    • Every app has an owner, and when they leave the app is handed over or switched off
    • Every manifest is written against one API version
    • Manifests expire after 90 days and the app has to be reinstalled
    • Unused permissions are flagged and removed
  • Roomer already shows versions, usage and one-click rollback per app

Roomer: AppOS in practice

  • Roomer books office pods for meetings or quiet work
  • Engineering owns the shell with sign-in, layout, data and permissions
  • Agents wrote four apps on top
    • Booking grid and Quick book for Product
    • Pod stats for Marketing
    • Pod admin for the Platform team
  • Each app is handed over as one .wasm with its manifest
  • Everything on the next slides runs today

Roomer example AppOS architecture

Example app: Booking grid

  • Book a pod in three steps: pick a pod, pick your hours, confirm
  • Written by an agent for Bob from Product, shipped as one .wasm
    • Bob can optimize, A/B test, layout changes, add features safely without engineering
    • Shipped without a manualcode review, the worst case is a wrong booking
  • Its manifest grants four permissions:
    • pods-read: list the pods
    • bookings-read: the day's bookings and bookable hours
    • bookings-write: book a pod, cancel only your own bookings
    • identity: who is booking

See running apps and permissions

WASM under the hood

  • Built with cargo for wasm32-wasip2
    • WebAssembly components of 55 to 150 KB
    • One export: request in, HTML out
  • At deploy the shell checks the imports against the manifest
    • A component lists the WIT interfaces it imports
    • Any import the manifest doesn't grant is refused
  • Each request gets a fresh wasmtime instance
    • Linked only to granted interfaces, no files, network or environment
    • Casbin checks every call: the app's grant and the user's role
    • Budget of 100 I/O units, 200 ms, 64 MB and CPU fuel, 8 parallel requests per app

Prior art

  • OSGi: bundles declare imports in a manifest, checked before anything runs
  • Portlets: the portal owns the page, each portlet renders a fragment
  • EAR: deployment descriptors declare security roles, the container enforces them
  • Browser extensions: declared permissions and store review
  • Atlassian Forge, Shopify, Salesforce: apps inside someone else's product
  • Firebase: untrusted code is fine if the rules hold
  • WebAssembly component model: capabilities as interfaces

Portals taught us the platform should own the page. OSGi taught us to check dependencies before anything runs. App stores taught us to review the submission up front.

What AppOS doesn't solve

  • Content, design and SEO stay with marketing
  • New APIs and new data still need engineering
  • An app can misuse what it is granted, like booking pods nobody needs
  • Apps can't call third-party services unless the shell offers an API for them
  • The shell team becomes a platform team

Where to start

  • Pick one app marketing wants to ship
  • Marketing and engineering write its manifest together
  • Put a shell in front that owns sign-in, layout and data
  • Without WASM, start with a plugin interface or a gateway with per-app tokens
  • Start with the import check, add fuzzing and gardening later
  • Engineering reviews the manifest instead of the code
